paras: The threatened lynching of John Cummins was an episode in Licking County, Ohio, in January 1881, when residents of Newark talked of lynching a farmer accused of torturing his seven-year-old son. No mob action against him was reported; he was bound over by a justice, tried in June, and fined $75. Papers across the country carried the case because of the nature of the punishment, and one later item described him as having been "almost lynched."

Cummins was described as a well-to-do farmer living near Amsterdam, or near Newark, who had "figured in the courts for years past" and whose wife had divorced him for alleged brutality. On a Saturday, about January 22, he punished his son for coasting against his orders by pinning the boy's tongue in a split stick with a tack and beating him in the stable. A second correspondent quoted by the Eaton Democrat gave a harsher version, in which the boy was nailed to the side of the barn from four in the afternoon until ten at night.

When the boy went to school the following Monday, his teacher drew the story from him and swore out a warrant, which Constable Taylor served. According to a Newark dispatch of January 26, Cummins gave a $500 bond, went home, and beat the boy again. A neighbor then warned Justice Anderson that the neighbors would "take the matter in their own hands," and the same dispatch said some citizens wished "to help lynch the scoundrel." The Fayette County Herald likewise reported that "lynching was freely talked of" in Newark, but no report describes a crowd gathering.

At a hearing before a justice on January 26, Cummins was held in $1,000 bail to a higher court, which he furnished. The Probate Court appointed the boy's uncle, Ham. Smith of Washington Court House, as his guardian. Tried in June, Cummins testified that he had used the stick "to make an impression on his mind," and he was fined $75.

Ohio and West Virginia papers framed the story around the father's cruelty, under headlines such as "A Fiendish Father" and "The Work of a Fiend," and passed on the lynching talk without comment. A Cincinnati wire carried the hearing to the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier, and news briefs ran as far as Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. In June and July the trial testimony was reprinted as a curiosity, and only the Daily Republican's version mentioned lynching at all. No report gives the race of Cummins, his son, or the citizens who threatened him.

The Newark reports of January describe only talk and threats, while the Daily Republican wrote in June that he had been "almost lynched," a later, non-local characterization with no supporting detail.

accounts.label: Fayette County Herald

accounts.label: Eaton Democrat (two correspondents)
accounts.gist: One correspondent had the tongue nailed to a stick tied to a manger for over two hours; another had the boy's thumbs pinned in a sapling and the boy nailed to the barn side from 4 p.m. to 10 p.m.

accounts.label: June trial report
accounts.gist: Described the man as 'almost lynched last January' and quoted his own testimony about the stick and tack.

framing.detail: Ohio and regional papers condemned the father ('A Fiendish Father', 'an inhuman brute', 'The Work of a Fiend') and passed on the lynching talk without comment.
Eastern and western papers ran the Cincinnati and Newark wires and later the trial testimony as brief curiosities.

conflicts.note: The January reports from Newark describe only talk and threats; the June item's 'almost lynched' is a later, non-local characterization with no supporting detail.

Cummins's farm near Newark (A5) or near Amsterdam (A1, A6), Licking County; hearing held at Newark.
The threatened man was John Cummins, a farmer; no race given. The child he was accused of torturing was his seven-year-old son, also unnamed by race.
Accused of cruel treatment of his seven-year-old son: pinning the boy's tongue in a split stick with a tack and beating him, as punishment for coasting.
Unnamed neighbors and Newark citizens who talked of taking matters into their own hands and of lynching.
